concept.name: At-the-money option
concept.definition: An at-the-money (ATM) option is an option whose strike price equals (or is nearest to) the current price of the underlying; in forward terms (ATMF) the strike equals the forward price. An ATM option has no intrinsic value — its entire premium is time value.
concept.intuition: The ATM option is the coin-flip strike: it sits exactly at the boundary between finishing valuable and finishing worthless, which makes it the most sensitive to volatility and time.
concept.mechanics: ATM options have delta near +0.5 (calls) or -0.5 (puts), the highest gamma and theta of the chain, and vega near its maximum. ATM implied volatility is the standard quoting benchmark from which skew/smile adjustments are measured.
concept.failure_modes: Because gamma and theta peak ATM, hedging errors and time-decay estimates are largest here, especially into expiration when tiny price moves flip the option between ITM and OTM (pin risk).
concept.misconceptions: ATM does not mean a 50/50 real-world probability of profit — the buyer must overcome the premium, so the breakeven lies beyond the strike; also, 'ATM spot' and 'ATM forward' strikes differ when rates or dividends are material.
concept.example: With stock at $100.10, the $100 strike is treated as at-the-money; its call might trade at $2.50, entirely time value.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
